column3: The Hebrew explicitly repeats Timnah’s name and calls the woman one of the Philistine daughters without an explicit word “young”; BSB names Timnah once and supplies “young.”
The Hebrew says he “went up”; BSB says he “returned.”
The Hebrew says “the daughters of your brothers” and “all my people”; BSB has “your relatives” and “any of our people.”
The Hebrew uses an unnamed “he” in the seeking clause; BSB identifies this subject as the LORD with a relative “who.”
The Hebrew uses plural “they came” for arriving at the vineyards; BSB continues with singular Samson as the subject.
The Hebrew says there was nothing in singular “his hand” and joins father and mother with “and”; BSB has “his bare hands” and “father or mother.”
The Hebrew explicitly names Samson in the pleasing clause and joins it with “and”; BSB leaves his name implicit and uses “because.”
The Hebrew explicitly repeats “the lion” with its body; BSB uses “it” for the second reference.
The Hebrew first refers to the honey with a pronoun and repeats the scooping verb later; BSB names the honey first and varies “scooped” and “taken.”
The Hebrew refers to what “young men” do in the plural; BSB describes a custom for singular “the bridegroom.”
The Hebrew leaves those who saw him unnamed; BSB supplies “the Philistines.”
The Hebrew repeats the telling verb for emphasis and separately says “and you find”; BSB combines these as “can solve it.”
The Hebrew says to tell or explain the riddle; BSB says “solve it.”
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew says “on the seventh day”; BSB says “on the fourth day.”
The Hebrew says the wife wept upon or against Samson without a separate coming verb; BSB adds that she “came to him.”
The Hebrew says he told her without an explicit noun “answer”; BSB supplies “the answer.”
The Hebrew says the men spoke “to him”; BSB explicitly names Samson.
The Hebrew leaves Samson unnamed here and ends with going up to his father’s house; BSB names him and describes the movement as returning.
The Hebrew actively describes the wife as becoming his companion’s wife without an explicit giving verb; BSB uses the passive “was given.”
